analysis.one_liner: Forces divesting very large mergers and lets agencies review smaller deals for improper approval.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 29, 2026 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote; it has five Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The CLEAN Mergers Act would reach back over mergers completed between January 20, 2025 and January 19, 2029 — the current presidential term. Any completed deal worth $10 billion or more would have to be unwound unless the companies could show it left markets concentrated, prices steady, and jobs consistent with what they promised regulators. Agencies or state attorneys general could also review smaller deals from that period and order divestiture if they find signs that the approval was influenced by political pressure, the revolving door, or conflicts of interest. It would also stretch the time limit for antitrust lawsuits from four years to ten, and add fines, court-appointed trustees to sell off assets, and a special counsel for criminal referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who face higher prices in concentrated markets, workers whose jobs depend on merger promises being kept, small businesses and startups that compete against large merged firms, and state attorneys general who gain a new tool to challenge tainted merger approvals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, workers, and small competitors of merged giants

how_it_helps.text: Deals of $10 billion or more completed during the covered period would have to be divested unless the companies prove the merger did not leave a market with a concentration score above 1,800, more than 30% market share, or a significant jump in concentration [S2].

Companies can only escape divestiture by showing prices and quality stayed in line with regulator representations, output and employment did not significantly fall, and prior divestitures were fully honored [S2].

Agencies or any state attorney general could review other transactions from the period and order divestiture if they find conditions such as clearance over the written objection of career staff, private ex-parte contacts by political appointees or lobbyists, conflicts of interest, statements by the President or Cabinet suggesting commitments were sought from acquirers, or revolving-door representation by a firm that recently employed an agency political appointee [S2].
The time limit for private antitrust suits would rise from four years to ten years, letting injured businesses and consumers reach further back for damages [S2].

Noncompliance would carry penalties of up to $100,000 per day or 5% of the deal value, courts could appoint an independent trustee to sell the assets, and knowingly staying merged could trigger triple damages [S2].
If there is probable cause that federal criminal laws were violated in a merger review, the Attorney General must appoint a special counsel to investigate and, if warranted, prosecute [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that closed large acquisitions during the current presidential term and their investors bear the cost of forced unwinding; corporate law firms and lobbyists lose fees as the bill sanctions lawyers, scrutinizes revolving-door representation, and requires preservation of all merger communications.
analysis.who_pays_short: Merged corporations, their investors, and their law firms

drawbacks.text: The divestiture mandate is retroactive: companies would be forced to unwind deals completed years earlier in reliance on then-current law, which creates legal uncertainty and can disrupt jobs, suppliers, and consumers tied to the merged operations [S2].

The grounds for finding improper influence are broad — including any statement by the President or a Cabinet member indicating a preference for an acquirer — which critics would say makes ordinary political speech about a merger review a trigger for unwinding a deal [S2].

The bill defines markets flexibly and makes divestiture the presumptive remedy, deferring to any plausible submarket without requiring direct evidence of price or output effects, which acquirers would argue lowers the bar for unwinding lawful deals too far [S2].

The bill includes a severability section providing that the rest of the Act survives if any provision is found unconstitutional — an acknowledgment that its authors expect legal challenges to its retroactive application [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — restoring competition and policing political interference in merger approvals — serves ordinary people directly, since concentrated markets tend to raise prices and depress wages. But the design is aggressive: it reopens completed deals on a four-year retroactive window with divestiture as the default, which guarantees years of litigation and uncertainty for the companies and workers inside those merged businesses. How well it would work depends heavily on how courts treat its broad definitions and retroactivity.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on April 29, 2026 on behalf of himself, Sens. Warren, Heinrich, Murphy, and Hirono [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
The full action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4].
The bill has four cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 45 Senate Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations that completed major mergers during the covered period are better off so far, since no review or unwinding has begun and the bill shows no signs of moving; the antitrust and lobbying bar also benefits from fees already earned on those deals remaining untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations whose big mergers remain unreviewed

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Martin Heinrich, Chris Murphy, and Mazie Hirono

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats and none of the Senate's 55 Republicans has signed on; the bill sits in a Judiciary Committee whose majority is Republican, and no member of that majority has taken any action on it.

industries.industry: Large corporations that completed major acquisitions in 2025-2029
industries.note: Any deal of $10 billion or more completed during the covered period would face automatic divestiture unless the companies could prove it met strict competition, price, output, and employment tests — the cost of unwinding deals is the price of restoring competition in the markets they consolidated. Their gain from staying merged is the higher prices consumers pay.

industries.industry: Corporate law firms and antitrust/lobbying bar
industries.note: The bill sanctions lawyers who fail document-preservation duties, disqualifies firms whose pro-bono work accompanied a settlement, and flags any firm that recently placed a political appointee at a reviewing agency. It targets the fee stream and influence channel that the merger-approval bar depends on.

Any state attorney general gets an unconditional right to intervene in exemption cases and independent authority to seek divestiture of tainted deals, giving state enforcers a new lever over national mergers.

analysis.trajectory: With five Democratic sponsors, no Republican support, and referral to a Republican-led Judiciary Committee in the final months of a Congress, the realistic path is the one most bills like this take: it stays in committee without a hearing or vote until the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Its best value to supporters is likely as a statement of the divestiture-and-revolving-door agenda rather than as a bill that becomes law.
